title: Oil and gas fields: recovery, gas-oil ratio, water cut, decline, emissions, blowouts, spacing and NZ field sizes

items.description: Ultimate oil recovery factor by reservoir drive mechanism (conventional reservoirs); columns are the low and high ends of the range
items.note: Table 'Recovery factors for different drive types', column 'Percent ultimate recovery - Oil': Strong water 45-60; Partial water 30-45; Gas expansion 20-30; Solution gas 15-25; Rock 10-60; Gravity drainage 50-70.

items.description: Ultimate gas recovery factor by reservoir drive mechanism; columns are the low and high ends of the range
items.note: Same table, column 'Gas': Strong water 30-40; Partial water 40-50; Gas expansion 50-70; Rock 60-80 (Solution gas and Gravity drainage listed N/A for gas).

items.description: Range of oil recovered by primary production alone
items.note: 'Usually, only 5 to 30 percent of a reservoir's original-oil-in-place (OOIP) can be recovered by primary production.'

items.description: Primary recovery of old solution-gas-drive New York oil fields
items.note: 'Primary production accounted for approximately 7 percent recovery of the OOIP in New York State's old oil fields.'

items.description: Average additional recovery from waterflooding over primary (New York old oil fields)
items.note: 'Secondary recovery by waterflooding has resulted in an average recovery of an additional 14 percent of the OOIP.' Primary 7 + 14 gives about 21 percent combined (derived).

items.description: Upper bound on additional oil recoverable by secondary techniques over primary
items.note: 'As much as 30 percent more of the OOIP may be recovered by supplementing primary energy with secondary recovery techniques.'

items.description: Upper limit of initial gas-oil ratio for black oil
items.note: 'It is characterized as having initial gas-oil ratios of 2000 scf/stb or less.' Lower bound not stated in this source.

items.description: Initial gas-oil ratio range for volatile (light) oil
items.note: 'Volatile oils generally have initial gas-oil ratios in the 2000 to 3300 scf/Bbl range, and the stock tank gravity is usually 40 API or higher.'

items.description: Worldwide average water produced per barrel of oil from depleting reservoirs (late-life field average)
items.note: 'Today, oil companies produce an average of three barrels of water for each barrel of oil from their depleting reservoirs.' Equivalent water cut 3/(3+1) = 75 percent (derived).

items.description: Worldwide daily water production accompanying oil production (210 / 75 = 2.8 bbl water per bbl oil)
items.note: 'worldwide daily water production of roughly 210 million barrels of water accompanying every 75 million barrels of oil'.

items.description: Observed annual decline rate of post-plateau giant oil fields (261 fields, end 2005); magnitudes, source prints as negative
items.note: Table 1: Decline rate -6.5% / -5.3% / -5.5% (Mean/Median/Prod. weight); Table 2: Land fields (170) -4.9% -4.4% -3.9%; Offshore fields (91) -9.4% -9.0% -9.7%.

items.description: IEA WEO 2008 production-weighted average decline rates by decline phase and field size (as tabulated by UKERC); phase 1 peak to end of plateau, phase 2 plateau to 50% of peak, phase 3 50% of peak to latest year
items.note: UKERC Table 4.4 'Production-weighted average decline rates by decline phase (%)', 'Source: IEA WEO 2008'.

items.description: IEA WEO 2008 global production-weighted observed decline rate for all post-peak fields
items.note: 'the IEA estimate a production-weighted global average decline rate of 6.7%/year for all post-peak fields.'

items.description: IEA WEO 2008 global production-weighted natural (no extra investment) decline rate of post-peak fields, 2003-2007
items.note: 'the global average production-weighted natural decline rate of all post-peak fields to be 9.0%/year. This is 2.3% higher than the estimated observed decline rate (6.7%/year).'

items.description: Typical Arps hyperbolic b exponent for conventional oil wells (b=0 exponential, b=1 harmonic)
items.note: 'b (typically 0.3-0.7 for oil wells)'; 'Typical b-factors: 0.3-0.7 for solution gas drive, 0.5-0.8 for water drive'; 'Validate b-factor is between 0 and 1'. Software documentation, not the primary Arps/Fetkovich papers.

items.description: Typical Arps b exponent for gas wells
items.note: 'Typical: 0.3-0.7 for oil, 0.5-1.0 for gas'.

items.description: Methane emitted by the US oil and gas supply chain as a fraction of gross gas production, 2015 (facility-based estimate 13 +/- 2 Tg/yr)
items.note: 'our facility-based estimate of 2015 supply chain emissions is 13 +/- 2 teragrams per year ... equivalent to 2.3% of gross U.S. gas production.' About 60% above the EPA inventory.

items.description: Blowout (total, incl. underground flow) frequency per well drilled, 1980-2011; columns US Gulf of Mexico OCS (31,574 wells) and North Sea (13,727 wells)
items.note: Table 3.1 and Table 4.1, row 'Blowout Total', columns Exploration/Development/All Drilling (per well): GOM 3.58E-03, 1.71E-03, 2.44E-03; North Sea 4.39E-03, 4.36E-04, 1.75E-03. Offshore data.

items.description: Blowout frequency per producing well-year, 1980-2011; columns US GOM (197,721 well-years) and North Sea (59,141 well-years)
items.note: Table 3.1 and 4.1 row 'Blowout Total': Oil Production 9.88E-05 (GOM), 2.50E-05 (NS); All Production 8.60E-05, 3.38E-05; Well Interventions 1.77E-04, 6.76E-05.

items.description: Well release (smaller loss-of-well-control, not full blowout) frequency, 1980-2011; columns US GOM and North Sea
items.unit: per well drilled or per well-year (see row)
items.note: Tables 3.1 and 4.1 row 'Well Release Total': All Drilling 1.01E-03 (GOM), 1.24E-03 (NS); All Production 2.02E-05, 1.69E-05.

items.description: Range of well spacing draining oil and gas formations in New York State
items.note: 'Most oil and gas formations in New York State are being drained by wells spaced from 1 to 160 acres.'

items.description: Statewide default well spacing rule (New York) and minimum distance between wells
items.note: 'Most wells must be spaced according to the statewide 40 acre spacing rule ... Under the 40 acre rule a well can be no closer than 1,320' from any other well completed in the same producing formation.'

items.description: Average output per well of a depleted solution-gas-drive field (western New York, 1912, about 7 percent of OOIP recovered)
items.unit: bbl oil per well per day
items.note: 'each well averaged only 1/8 to 1/10 barrel of oil per day and it was estimated only 7 percent of the original oil in place had been recovered'. Historical stripper-well illustration only.

items.description: Methane perturbation lifetime (e-folding time of a pulse including the feedback of methane on its own lifetime); used for emissions metrics
items.note: Table 7.15 (p. 1017): 'CH4-fossil 11.8 ± 1.8' and 'CH4-non fossil 11.8 ± 1.8' (Lifetime, Years; ±1.8 is the assessed uncertainty). Sec. 7.6.1: 'The perturbation lifetimes of CH4 (Section 6.3.1). and N2O (Section 5.2.3.1) have been slightly revised since AR5 to be 11.8 ± 1.8 years'. Ch. 6 sec. 6.3.1 (ipcc_ar6_wg1_ch6): 'This results in an overall perturbation methane lifetime of 11.8 ± 1.8 years, within the range of the AR5 value of 12.4 ± 1.4 years.'

items.description: Methane total atmospheric lifetime (burden over total sinks), AR6 assessed value
items.note: Table 6.2 (printed p. 836), row 'AR6 assessed value': Total Chemical Lifetime '9.7 ± 1.1', Soil Lifetime '135 ± 44', Total Atmospheric Lifetime '9.1 ± 0.9' years ('Based on top-down with uncertainty estimate from AR5'; footnote: 'Uncertainties indicate ± 1 standard deviation'). CMIP6 (Stevenson et al.) total 8.0 (7.7-8.2); bottom-up 8.0 (6.3-10.0).
